commodity fetishism.definition: Karl Marx defined commodity fetishism as the perception of social relationships involved in production as economic relationships among money and commodities traded in market exchange.

options.title: Childhood headbands and peer conformity
options.preview: Wanting the exact same headband as every other girl in elementary school revealed how products take on social power.

options.title: Construction repairs after a hurricane
options.preview: Watching a construction worker rebuild a damaged house every day highlighted how workers are treated as cheap commodities.

cohabitation.definition: Cohabitation is the practice of unmarried couples living together in a romantic relationship, often as a precursor or alternative to marriage.

options.title: Military benefits and future marriage
options.preview: Reflecting on childhood with unmarried parents, discussions begin with a military boyfriend about moving in together on base and getting married.

options.title: Testing relationships before marriage
options.preview: Evaluating current trends shows couples moving in together to test compatibility before making a legal commitment to marry.

options.title: College peers living together
options.preview: Observing classmates living with significant others highlights how unmarried couples share living spaces as an alternative to early marriage.

options.title: Choosing partnership without marriage
options.preview: Considering rising wedding costs and divorce rates explains why long-term couples choose to live together without signing marriage licenses.

social solidarity.definition: Social solidarity refers to the ties that bind a society together, categorized by Émile Durkheim into mechanical and organic forms.

options.title: Military culture and civilian life
options.preview: Returning to college after military service revealed how deeply shared symbols and wartime bonds united fellow veterans.

options.title: Preparing for a bar mitzvah
options.preview: Studying prayers and playing piano at retirement homes showed how religious rituals connect individuals to a wider community.

options.title: Faith and church community
options.preview: Growing up in a religious household and attending parish events showed how shared beliefs bind people into close social circles.

options.title: Questioning childhood religious beliefs
options.preview: Questioning long-held religious traditions caused friction with devout family and friends who relied on faith for social cohesion.

systemic racism.definition: Systemic racism is institutional policies and cultural practices that reinforce racial inequality across society, as described by Joe Feagin.

options.title: Police talks and ballet spaces
options.preview: Growing up learning strict rules for interactions with police officers revealed structural racial inequalities that peers never faced.

options.title: Adoption and contrasting racial experiences
options.preview: Living with adopted younger siblings from Ethiopia highlighted stark differences in school isolation and safety concerns.

options.title: Moving to a predominantly white campus
options.preview: Leaving a diverse military community to attend university exposed institutional disparities and stories of exclusion from peers of color.

options.title: Job hunting with a friend
options.preview: Watching a qualified friend get passed over for a retail position exposed unearned racial advantages in the local job market.

options.title: Differing family opportunities after school
options.preview: Comparing post-graduation engineering plans with an immigrant friend's career prospects demonstrated how generational wealth shapes life chances.

rationalization.definition: Max Weber defined rationalization as the replacement of traditions and values with efficiency, calculation, and bureaucratic control in modern society.

options.title: Choosing higher pay over passions
options.preview: Facing post-college job choices, a brother accepts a high-paying, unfulfilling position over his personal passion due to economic expectations.

options.title: Cost and cremation over funerals
options.preview: Analyzing modern end-of-life choices reveals how families often select direct cremation purely for speed, efficiency, and lower expenses.

options.title: Standardized care in modern clinics
options.preview: Visiting medical offices highlights how digital check-in kiosks and rigid appointment schedules process patients like fast-food customers.

options.title: Drive-thrus and order-ahead apps
options.preview: Rushing through everyday routines shows how drive-thrus and self-checkouts replace traditional interactions with calculated efficiency.

options.title: Camp counseling versus financial return
options.preview: Working for low pay at a beloved summer camp shows the contrast between meaningful work and jobs rewarded purely by financial calculation.

backstage.definition: Erving Goffman defined the backstage as a private space where individuals relax, drop their social masks, and prepare for future performances.

options.title: Family illness and public composure
options.preview: Masking personal fear and grief at high school while family members quietly dropped their cheerful fronts only inside their home.

options.title: Conforming at Christian high school
options.preview: Preparing each morning to put on a deeply religious act for teachers and peers before finally taking it off in private.

options.title: Hiding depression with friends
options.preview: Going out bowling and presenting a cheerful front to friends while privately dealing with severe emotional distress.

options.title: Dropping roles when alone
options.preview: Shifting between different expectations for family and friends, then dropping all social facades when sitting alone in a room.

other.definition: The Other is any group or individual defined by the dominant group as fundamentally different or alien, a concept expanded by Simone de Beauvoir and Edward Said.

options.title: High school weight training class
options.preview: Enrolling as the only female in a weight training class led to isolation and hostile remarks from male peers and a substitute teacher.

options.title: Job hunting for manual labor
options.preview: Applying for a warehouse position at a local feed store led to immediate rejection when the owner told her to work the register.

options.title: Door security at fraternity parties
options.preview: Arriving at a campus fraternity party resulted in fraternity members inspecting the group of women and abruptly turning one away.

options.title: Pay disparity at summer camp
options.preview: Comparing pay rates with coworkers revealed that female staff members were paid less than their male counterparts despite having more experience.

options.title: Dynamics in male friend groups
options.preview: Hanging out as the only straight woman in a male friend group led to feeling objectified and excluded from equal social standing.

anomie.definition: Anomie is a condition of moral instability and normlessness resulting from a breakdown in social standards, as theorized by Émile Durkheim.

options.title: Changing norms and dating rules
options.preview: Shifting expectations around dating and family roles made dating conventions confusing while altering traditional social expectations.

options.title: Societal change and modern meaning
options.preview: Comparing classical sociological theory with modern texts revealed how rapid changes in religion and technology leave people feeling normless.
